$comment: Which benchmark runs the website is allowed to show, and in what order.
Explicit rather than a glob over eval/results/. A glob would publish whatever
happened to be on disk — a smoke run, an aborted sweep, a re-run left over from
debugging — and the difference between 'a run exists' and 'this run is the one
we stand behind' is exactly the difference this file records.
Adding a row is a decision. The sync script reads the run's own metrics.json
and refuses to publish a row whose directory is missing, so a deleted run
fails the build instead of silently vanishing from the page.
Order is editorial: the result with real negatives goes first, because it is
the only one that supports a precision and a reader should meet it before the
recall-only ones. Nothing here reorders by how good the numbers are.

runs.why: The only corpus here with real negatives, so the only one that can support a precision, a false-positive rate or an F1.
Real upstream prose from 1,511 annotated npm breaking changes, against the production prose interpreter.
The binary form of the same question, published mainly for its trivial-marker baseline: the labels are close to regex-recoverable, and the comparison says so.

Every task in swe-bump-bench, run against the same engine as the Java and Python corpora here. Comparing rates across runs of different vintages is unsound, so the three consumer-impact corpora are re-run together whenever the engine moves.

BUMP's Java consumer breakages in full — every record in the corpus, evaluated on the real historical commit pair, not a stratified subset. Replaces the 40-case sample: a false-safe rate is the number this page treats as blocking a general-availability claim, and it deserves the whole corpus behind it rather than a sample that invites the question of which 40.
TimeMachine's human-verified migration failures, run against the same engine as the Java and TypeScript corpora here — see the note on swe-bump-full.
